collection_intro: Short, ungraded practice checks, one for each section of Chapter 4 of *Java Programming*, 10th edition. Rate your confidence, answer, and read the feedback: the review at the end points you to exactly what to re-read.

checks.title: Learning About Classes and Objects
checks.subtitle: Classes versus objects, is-a relationships, shared methods with different arguments, and class clients
checks.intro: A classmate defines a fish as "a goldfish named Moby." Five questions on what a class is, what an object is, and how the two relate.
takeaways: A class is the general description (the attributes and methods every member has); an object is one concrete instance of it. Read *is-a* from object to class: "Moby is a `Fish`," never the reverse.
Every object of a class has the same methods, but each object keeps its own attribute values and receives its own arguments when you call those methods.

questions.stem: Your goldfish is named Moby, and a program has a `Fish` class. Which sentence describes their relationship correctly?

options.text: Moby is an instance of the `Fish` class.
options.feedback: An object is one concrete example of a class, so the is-a statement runs from the specific object (Moby) to the general class (`Fish`).

options.text: The `Fish` class is an instance of Moby.
options.feedback: This reverses the relationship. The class is the general description; Moby is one tangible example of it.

options.text: Moby is a `Fish`, so `Fish` describes only goldfish.
options.feedback: A class is more general than any one member. Your goldfish, a guppy and a shark are all instances of `Fish`, so one object can't define the class.

options.text: Moby and `Fish` are both classes, since both have attributes.
options.feedback: Having attributes doesn't make something a class. Moby is a single object; `Fish` is the class that gives Moby its attributes.

questions.hint: Which of the two is general, and which is one tangible example?
questions.explanation: A class is abstract and general; an object is concrete and specific. An is-a statement is correct only in the order object → class: "my oak desk is a `Desk`," not "a `Desk` is my oak desk."
questions.aside: Classes and objects were first introduced in Simula 67, a language created in Norway by Ole-Johan Dahl and Kristen Nygaard to write simulations. Java's object model descends from that idea, by way of Smalltalk and C++.

questions.stem: A student writes: "A class is an instantiation of many objects." What is wrong with the statement?

options.text: It reverses the idea: an object is one instantiation of a class.
options.feedback: Instantiation produces objects *from* a class. The class comes first, as the description, and each object is one instance of it.

options.text: Nothing: a class is assembled from the objects that are created from it.
options.feedback: Objects don't build their class. Objects gain their attributes and methods *from* the class.

options.text: A class can be an instantiation of one object only, not many.
options.feedback: This keeps the backward direction and only changes the count. A class isn't an instantiation of objects at all.

options.text: The word should be inheritance: a class inherits many objects.
options.feedback: Inheritance relates one class to another (a goldfish is also a `Vertebrate`), not a class to its objects.

questions.hint: Which comes first, the class or the objects made from it?
questions.explanation: A class is the blueprint and each object is one instantiation of it. Many objects can be instantiated from one class, and each gets its attributes and methods from that class.

questions.stem: `Party` has a `setDate()` method that stores a date and a `getDate()` method that returns it. What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `May 12 / June 3`
options.feedback: Both objects use the same `setDate()` method, but each call sends its own argument, and each object keeps its own date.

options.text: `June 3 / June 3`
options.feedback: This treats the date as one value shared by every `Party`. Each object has its own date, so setting `yours` doesn't touch `mine`.

options.text: `May 12 / May 12`
options.feedback: This assumes the first date set becomes the date for the whole class. Each object receives its own argument.

options.text: Compile error: two objects can't share one `setDate()` method
options.feedback: Every object of a class is assumed to possess the same methods; that sharing is the point of a class.

questions.hint: When you send a message to `yours`, which object's date changes?
questions.explanation: All instances of a class have the same methods, but calling a method on one object affects that object. The arguments you send to one object's methods can differ from those you send to another's.

questions.stem: A veterinary clinic's program creates objects from a `Dog` class that another programmer wrote. What does the reading call the clinic's program?

options.text: A class client of `Dog`
options.feedback: An application or class that instantiates objects of another class is a class client, or class user.

options.text: An instance of `Dog`
options.feedback: Instances are the objects created from `Dog`. The clinic's program creates them; it isn't one of them.

options.text: An extension of the `Dog` class
options.feedback: Extending a class means building a new class on top of it through inheritance. Creating `Dog` objects is just using the class.

options.text: A constructor of `Dog`
options.feedback: A constructor is a special method inside a class that builds its objects. The clinic's program calls it but isn't one.

questions.hint: What do you call a program that *uses* a class someone else wrote?
questions.explanation: You don't have to write every class you use. A program that instantiates objects of a class written elsewhere is that class's client.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.1, class client or class user (p. 117)

questions.concept: Classes that run versus classes that model
questions.stem: `Employee` has fields and get/set methods but no `main()`. `Payroll` creates `Employee` objects inside its `main()`. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: `Payroll` is an application; `Employee` exists for other classes to use.
options.feedback: A class with `public static void main()` is an application. `Employee` is written so that classes like `Payroll` can instantiate it.

options.text: Both can be run as programs, because every Java class is an application.
options.feedback: Only a class with a `main()` method is a starting point you can run. `Employee` compiles but can't be executed.

options.text: Neither can run until `Employee` also gets a `main()` method.
options.feedback: `Employee` doesn't need its own `main()`; `Payroll`'s `main()` is the starting point and uses `Employee` objects.

options.text: `Employee` is the application, because `Payroll` depends on it.
options.feedback: Depending on a class doesn't make that class the application. The class with `main()` is where execution starts.

questions.hint: Where does execution start in a Java application?
questions.explanation: Some classes are applications that run, some describe objects for other classes to instantiate, and some do both. Only a class with `main()` can be executed.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.1, Notes on classes with main() (p. 117)

checks.title: Creating a Class
checks.subtitle: Class headers, data fields, instance variables versus static fields, and private data with public methods
checks.intro: Two `Ticket` objects seem to overwrite each other's data, but only some of it. Five questions on what goes inside a class and who owns each field.
takeaways: A class header is an optional access specifier, the keyword `class` and an identifier. Data fields are variables declared inside the class but outside every method.
Without `static`, every object gets its own copy of a field (an instance variable). With `static`, one copy exists for the whole class and every object shares it.
Fields are usually `private` and methods usually `public`, so other classes can reach the data only through the class's own methods (information hiding).

questions.stem: Which is a legal class header that follows Java conventions?

options.text: `public class Employee`
options.feedback: An optional access specifier, then the keyword `class`, then an identifier that starts with an uppercase letter.

options.text: `public Employee class`
options.feedback: The keyword `class` must come before the identifier, not after it.

options.text: `public class Employee()`
options.feedback: Parentheses belong to method and constructor headers. A class header ends with the identifier.

options.text: `public void class Employee`
options.feedback: `void` is a method return type. A class has no return type.

questions.hint: What three parts make up a class header, and in what order?
questions.explanation: A class header has an optional access specifier, the keyword `class` and a legal identifier, conventionally starting with an uppercase letter. The body, between braces, holds the fields and methods.

questions.concept: What counts as a data field
questions.stem: Which variables in this class are data fields?

code.label: Java

options.text: `price` and `name`
options.feedback: Both are declared inside the class but outside any method. Their position before or after the method doesn't matter.

options.text: `price` only, because fields must come before the methods
options.feedback: Fields are conventionally listed first, but Java lets you place fields and methods in any order. `name` is still a field.

options.text: `price`, `tax` and `name`
options.feedback: `tax` is declared inside `setPrice()`, so it is a local variable of that method, not a field of the class.

options.text: `price`, `p`, `tax` and `name`
options.feedback: `p` is a parameter and `tax` a local variable. Both exist only while `setPrice()` runs.

questions.hint: For each variable, is it declared inside a method or directly in the class body?
questions.explanation: Data fields are variables declared within a class but outside of any method. Variables declared inside a method, including its parameters, belong to that method only.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `shared` is `static`, so one copy exists and `b.set(9)` overwrites it. `own` is an instance variable, so `a` keeps its own 5.
This treats both fields as belonging to `a` alone. A `static` field is one value for the whole class, so `b`'s call changed it.
This treats both fields as shared. Without `static`, each object gets its own copy of `own`.
This swaps the two fields' behavior. The `static` one is shared and changed by `b`; the nonstatic one belongs to `a`.

questions.hint: How many copies of `shared` exist after two `Ticket` objects are created? How many of `own`?
questions.explanation: Each object gets its own copy of every nonstatic field, which is why those are called instance variables. A `static` field occurs once per class, and all objects share its single value.
questions.aside: Java lets you reach a `static` field through an object, as in `a.shared`, which hides the fact that it's shared; `javac -Xlint` warns about it. C# refuses outright (error CS0176) and makes you write the class name instead.

questions.stem: Why are a class's fields usually `private` while its methods are usually `public`?

options.text: Outside classes can reach the data only through methods that control it.
options.feedback: Like a receptionist in front of a private office, the public methods decide what goes in and what comes out of the private data.

options.text: Private fields use less memory, and public methods run faster.
options.feedback: Access specifiers don't change memory use or speed. They control which classes may use a member.

options.text: Private fields can't be changed by anything, so the data stays fixed.
options.feedback: That describes `final`. A class's own methods can still change its private fields.

options.text: Java requires it: a public field causes a compile error.
options.feedback: A field may be public (`Math.PI` is). Private fields are a design choice that protects the data.

questions.hint: Who is allowed to touch a `private` field, and who controls what they can do with it?
questions.explanation: Private access means only the class's own methods can set, get or use a field. Pairing private data with public methods is information hiding: clients go through methods that can check and shape every request.
questions.aside: Python has no `private` keyword. A leading underscore (`_balance`) is only a convention meaning "internal, please don't touch," and the language doesn't enforce it. In Java the compiler rejects outside access to a `private` field.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.2, private data and public methods (p. 118)

questions.concept: Fields that are public, static and final
questions.stem: You want a sales-tax rate that any program can read without creating an object, and that can never change. Which declaration fits?

options.text: `public static final double RATE = 0.07;`
options.feedback: `public` lets any class read it, `static` means no object is needed, and `final` stops it from changing, just like `Math.PI`.

options.text: `public static double RATE = 0.07;`
options.feedback: This can be read without an object, but without `final` any class could assign it a new value.

options.text: `public final double RATE = 0.07;`
options.feedback: This can't change, but without `static` each object has its own copy, so you'd need an object to read it.

options.text: `private static final double RATE = 0.07;`
options.feedback: This is shared and fixed, but `private` hides it from every other class.

questions.hint: Which keyword removes the need for an object, and which one prevents changes?
questions.explanation: Occasionally a field should be public. When a value must be usable without an object and must never change, declare it `static` and `final` as well, as Java does for `Math.PI`.

checks.title: Creating Instance Methods in a Class
checks.subtitle: Getters and setters, instance methods versus class methods, and which calls another class may make
checks.intro: `Counter.addOne();` refuses to compile, and the error mentions a "static context." Six questions on the methods that belong to objects.
takeaways: Setters (mutator methods) change field values and usually return `void`; getters (accessor methods) return a field's value. The `set` and `get` prefixes are a convention, not a rule.
Methods that work with one object's fields are instance methods: no `static`, and they must be called with an object. `static` methods are class methods.
From another class, a `private` member can't be used at all, and a nonstatic method also needs an object. Inside its own class, a method uses the fields directly.

questions.stem: A class has a `private double price;` field. Which pair of headers is right for its getter and setter?

options.text: `public double getPrice()` and `public void setPrice(double p)`
options.feedback: The getter returns the field's type and needs no input; the setter receives the new value and returns nothing.

options.text: `public void getPrice()` and `public double setPrice(double p)`
options.feedback: The return types are swapped. A getter must return the value it retrieves, so it can't be `void`.

options.text: `public static double getPrice()` and `public static void setPrice(double p)`
options.feedback: Each object has its own `price`, so its getter and setter must be instance methods, without `static`.

options.text: `public double getPrice(double p)` and `public void setPrice()`
options.feedback: The parameters are swapped. The setter is the one that needs the new value as input.

questions.hint: Which method needs a value coming in, and which one sends a value back?
questions.explanation: A mutator (setter) takes the new value as a parameter and usually returns `void`. An accessor (getter) takes nothing and returns the field's type. Neither is `static` when each object has its own field.
questions.aside: Many Java tools rely on these names. By the JavaBeans convention, a `boolean` field's getter may also be named with `is`, as in `isActive()`, and frameworks discover an object's properties by looking for `get`, `set` and `is` methods.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.3, mutator and accessor methods and Figure 4-2 (p. 119)

questions.stem: Another class has `MyClass obj = new MyClass();`. In which list do **all three** calls compile?

code.label: Java

options.text: `obj.pubInst();`, `obj.pubStat();`, `MyClass.pubStat();`
options.feedback: All three methods are public. The nonstatic one is called with an object, and a static method can be called with an object or with the class name.

options.text: `obj.pubInst();`, `MyClass.pubStat();`, `MyClass.pubInst();`
options.feedback: `MyClass.pubInst()` uses the class name for a nonstatic method. Instance methods need an object.

options.text: `obj.pubInst();`, `obj.privInst();`, `MyClass.pubStat();`
options.feedback: `obj.privInst()` fails: a private method can't be called from outside its class, even through an object.

options.text: `obj.pubStat();`, `MyClass.pubStat();`, `MyClass.privStat();`
options.feedback: `MyClass.privStat()` fails. Being static removes the need for an object, but private still hides it.

questions.hint: Ask two questions of each call: is the method visible from outside, and does it need an object?
questions.explanation: From another class, only public members are usable. A static method can be called through the class name or an object; a nonstatic method requires an object.

questions.stem: What happens when you compile `CounterApp`?

code.label: Java

options.text: Compile error: `addOne()` needs a `Counter` object
options.feedback: Calling through the class name works only for `static` methods. An instance method must be called through an object, such as `c.addOne()`.

options.text: It compiles, and the call sets `count` to 1
options.feedback: No `Counter` object exists, so there is no `count` to change. The compiler rejects the call.

options.text: Compile error: `count` is used before it has a value
options.feedback: Fields get automatic starting values (0 for an `int`), so `count + 1` is legal inside the class.

options.text: It compiles, but the call does nothing because no object exists
options.feedback: Java doesn't let this reach run time. The compiler checks that nonstatic methods are called with an object.

questions.hint: Is `addOne()` declared `static`? What must sit in front of the dot to call it?
questions.explanation: You can't use a nonstatic method without an object. Methods that belong to objects are instance methods; only `static` (class) methods can be called through the class name.

questions.stem: You create 100 `Employee` objects. How many copies of the nonstatic `getEmpNum()` method exist in memory?

options.text: One, shared by every `Employee` object
options.feedback: Nonstatic fields are copied for each object, but methods are not. Each call is told which object is using it.

options.text: 100, one per object, since each returns its own number
options.feedback: Each object has its own `empNum`, but storing 100 identical copies of the method's code would waste memory.

options.text: None until the method is called for the first time
options.feedback: The method's code is part of the class. It isn't created or copied when it's called.

options.text: 101: one for the class plus one for each object
options.feedback: Only fields are allocated per object. The class's single copy of the method serves every object.

questions.hint: What differs from object to object: the method's code or the data it reads?
questions.explanation: Memory for nonstatic fields is allocated once per object, but only one copy of each method exists, static or not. A nonstatic method still behaves uniquely for each object because each call tells it which object to work with.

questions.stem: A teammate says: "Methods without `static` are class methods, because they're written in the class." Which correction is accurate?

options.text: Nonstatic methods are instance methods; `static` ones are class methods.
options.feedback: The terms follow ownership: methods used with object instantiations are instance methods, and classwide (`static`) methods are class methods.

options.text: The teammate is right: any method written in a class is a class method.
options.feedback: Every method is written in a class, so that can't be what the term means. It names the `static` ones.

options.text: Nonstatic methods are accessor methods, and static ones are mutators.
options.feedback: Accessor and mutator describe whether a method gets or sets a value. Either kind can be static or not.

options.text: Only methods whose names start with `get` or `set` are instance methods.
options.feedback: The prefixes are a naming convention. Any method without `static` is an instance method.

questions.hint: Does the method belong to individual objects, or to the class as a whole?
questions.explanation: `static` marks classwide methods (class methods). Methods without it belong to objects and are called instance methods; there is no `nonstatic` keyword, because nonstatic is the default.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.3, Two Truths & a Lie and Table 4-1 (pp. 120, 123)

questions.stem: A student writes `public double getPrice(double price)` and explains: "The getter needs the field passed in so it can return it." What's the flaw?

options.text: Every method in the class already sees `price`; no parameter is needed.
options.feedback: When a class contains fields and methods, each method has direct access to every field, so the getter just returns it.

options.text: There is none: a getter must receive the field it returns.
options.feedback: A getter's caller usually doesn't know the value; that's why it calls the getter. Requiring it as input defeats the purpose.

options.text: The getter should be `static` so that it can see the field directly.
options.feedback: It's the reverse: a `static` method can't use an instance field directly. A getter for each object's `price` must be nonstatic.

options.text: The return type should be `void`, because the value is passed in.
options.feedback: A getter's whole job is to return the value, so it needs a return type that matches the field.

questions.hint: Inside a class, what can a method see without being handed anything?
questions.explanation: A class's methods don't need to receive the class's own fields as parameters or return values to its own fields. Every method in the class has direct access to every field.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.3, Figure 4-6 (pp. 122–123), and Don't Do It (p. 153)

checks.title: Declaring Objects and Using Their Methods
checks.subtitle: Declaring a reference, allocating with new, constructors, and data hiding with set and get
checks.intro: `clerk.empNum = 789;` looks harmless, yet it won't compile. Five questions on creating objects and reaching their data.
takeaways: `Employee e;` only declares a reference. `new Employee()` allocates the object and calls its constructor, and the reference then holds the object's memory address.
Other classes reach private fields only through public methods. A setter can reject invalid values and a getter can control what is returned, which is why encapsulation beats a public field.

questions.stem: After the statement `Employee someEmployee;` runs, what exists?

options.text: Only a name known to refer to an `Employee`; no object yet
options.feedback: For a class type, the declaration only announces the identifier. Memory for the object is set aside when `new` runs.

options.text: An `Employee` object whose fields hold their default values
options.feedback: Default values are given when an object is constructed. Without `new`, nothing has been constructed.

options.text: An `Employee` object built by the automatic constructor
options.feedback: The constructor runs only as part of `new Employee()`, which this statement doesn't contain.

options.text: Memory for the `Employee` object, but not yet for its fields
options.feedback: Memory is reserved automatically only for primitive variables. An object's memory, fields included, comes from `new`.

questions.hint: Which part of the two-step process creates the object?
questions.explanation: Creating an object takes two steps: declare a type and identifier, then allocate memory with `new`. Unlike `int someValue;`, declaring an object reserves no memory for the object itself.
questions.aside: Printing an object whose class doesn't define `toString()` shows something like `Employee@1b6d3586`. The part after `@` is a hash code in hexadecimal, not the actual memory address; Java never lets you see or do arithmetic on the addresses its references hold.

questions.stem: `Employee` declares `private int empNum;` and public `setEmpNum()` and `getEmpNum()` methods. What happens when you compile this?

code.label: Java

error_contains: empNum has private access in Employee

options.text: Compile error: `empNum` has private access in `Employee`
options.feedback: Only `Employee`'s own methods may use its private field. A client must call `clerk.setEmpNum(789)`.

options.text: It compiles, and the clerk's number becomes 789
options.feedback: That would work only if `empNum` were public. Private fields can't be assigned from another class.

options.text: It compiles, but the value is ignored at run time
options.feedback: The compiler enforces private access, so the program never gets to run.

options.text: Compile error: `clerk` must call `getEmpNum()` before setting a value
options.feedback: Methods can be called in any order. The problem is reaching the field directly.

questions.hint: Which classes are allowed to use a `private` field?
questions.explanation: A client can't access a private field directly; it must use the class's public methods. That is data hiding, an important principle of object-oriented programming.

questions.stem: In `Employee someEmployee = new Employee();`, what is `Employee()` after `new`?

options.text: A constructor that creates and initializes the object
options.feedback: It looks like a method call because it is one: a special method that constructs objects, always named after its class.

options.text: A getter that returns the class's fields
options.feedback: Getters are ordinary methods called on an existing object. Here no object exists until this call builds it.

options.text: The identifier that will name the new object
options.feedback: The identifier is `someEmployee`. `Employee()` is what builds the object the identifier will refer to.

options.text: A cast that converts the newly allocated memory to an `Employee`
options.feedback: A cast looks like `(Employee)`, with the type inside parentheses. This is a method call with empty parentheses.

questions.hint: What special method always has the same name as its class?
questions.explanation: A constructor is a special method that creates and initializes objects, and its name always matches its class. If you write none, Java supplies one.

questions.stem: A student asks: "If a public method can set `empNum` anyway, what does keeping the field private add?" Which answer reflects the reading?

options.text: A setter can reject invalid IDs; a getter can control what's returned.
options.feedback: The public methods are where rules live: "at least five digits," "starts with a 9," or adding a company code before returning an ID.

options.text: There's no real difference; `private` is only a style convention in Java.
options.feedback: The compiler enforces `private`, and the methods give the class a place to validate and control its data.

options.text: A public field can be read by other classes but not assigned.
options.feedback: A public field can be both read and assigned by any class. That's why it offers no protection.

options.text: A public field would be shared by every `Employee` object.
options.feedback: Sharing comes from `static`, not `public`. A public instance field is still one per object.

questions.hint: What could a set method do with the value before storing it?
questions.explanation: Private data with public methods lets a class enforce rules on what is stored and how it's retrieved. Even when there are no rules yet, the methods make adding them later easy.
questions.aside: C# builds this pattern into the language with properties: `public int EmpNum { get; set; }` reads like a field to clients but runs get and set code, so validation can be added later without changing any client.

questions.concept: Each object holds its own values
questions.stem: `SpaService` has a `private double price;` field with `setPrice()` and `getPrice()`. What does this print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `second` received 30.0 + 15 = 45.0 when its setter ran. Changing `first` later doesn't reach back into `second`.
This assumes `second`'s price stays linked to `first`'s. The getter returned a number, and `second` stored a copy of that number.
This forgets that `first.setPrice(20.0)` replaced the first value. A field holds its most recent value.
The prices are `double` values, which Java displays with a decimal point.

questions.hint: What value did `second` store at the moment its `setPrice()` ran?
questions.explanation: Each object keeps its own field values, changed only through its own methods. Passing one object's getter result to another object's setter copies a value; it doesn't connect the objects.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.4, You Do It: Declaring and Using Objects (pp. 127–128)

checks.title: Understanding That Classes Are Data Types
checks.subtitle: Abstract and composite data types, and passing objects into and out of methods
checks.intro: `main()` declares an `Employee` but never uses `new`, and the program still works. Five questions on classes as types you invent.
takeaways: A class you write is a programmer-defined, composite data type: it is built from smaller parts, and as an abstract data type its implementation is hidden behind public methods.

Objects can be declared, passed to methods, returned from methods and assigned, just like primitive values. What travels is the reference, so a method that receives an object can change that same object.

questions.stem: Why can a class you create be called an abstract data type (ADT)?

options.text: Its implementation is hidden; clients use it through its public methods.
options.feedback: That is the reading's definition: clients work with the type through its public interface without seeing how it's built.

options.text: It can't be used to create objects until some other class extends it first.
options.feedback: That describes Java's `abstract` keyword, a different idea. Your `Employee` class is an ADT and can be instantiated.

options.text: It has methods but no fields, so it contains no actual data.
options.feedback: An ADT normally has fields; they're just hidden from clients behind its methods.

options.text: It is one of the built-in types that Java's creators defined.
options.feedback: Built-in types like `int` are primitive. A class you create is a programmer-defined type.

questions.hint: What does a client of your class see, and what does it not see?
questions.explanation: An abstract data type is a type whose implementation is hidden and accessed through its public methods. A class you write is also a programmer-defined type, because it isn't built into the language.

questions.stem: Why is `Employee` called a composite type while `int` is called a scalar type?

options.text: `Employee` is built from smaller parts, its fields; an `int` has no parts.
options.feedback: A composite type is composed of smaller pieces. An `int` is a single whole-number value.

options.text: An `int` takes four bytes of memory, while composite types always take eight.
options.feedback: An `int` is four bytes, but an object's size depends on its fields. Size isn't what composite means.

options.text: An `int` can be passed to methods, but a composite type can't.
options.feedback: Objects can be passed to and returned from methods just like primitives.

options.text: Java defines `int`, and anything a programmer defines is scalar.
options.feedback: It's the other way around: the built-in primitives are the scalar types, and your classes are composite.

questions.hint: What is an `Employee` made of?
questions.explanation: Primitive types such as `int` and `double` are scalar: single values the language already defines. A class is composite: it is composed of fields and methods you choose.

questions.concept: Returning an object from a method
questions.stem: What does this program print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `makeEmployee()` builds an object, sets its number and returns it; `main()` assigns the returned object to `worker`.

options.text: `ID 0`
options.feedback: This assumes `temp`'s object disappears when the method ends. The object survives because its reference is returned.

options.text: Compile error: a method can't return an object
options.feedback: A method's return type can be a class. `Employee` is used here exactly like `int` would be.

options.text: Compile error: `worker` must be created with `new` first
options.feedback: `worker` receives an object that was already created inside `makeEmployee()`.

questions.hint: Where is the `Employee` constructed, and how does it get to `main()`?
questions.explanation: A class is a data type, so a method can declare it as its return type. The object constructed inside the method is handed back, and the caller can assign it to a reference of the same type.

questions.concept: Passing an object to a method
questions.stem: What does this program print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `raise()` receives a reference to the same object `emp` refers to, so its setter changes that object's salary.
This applies the primitive rule from Chapter 3, where a method gets a copy of the value. Here the copy is a reference to the same object.
The salary is a `double`, so Java prints it with a decimal point.

options.text: Compile error: `raise()` must return the changed `Employee`
options.feedback: Returning the object is allowed but not needed: the method already changed the object `emp` refers to.

questions.hint: When `emp` is passed, does `raise()` get a new `Employee` or a way to reach the same one?
questions.explanation: An object name is a reference that holds a memory address. Passing an object passes that reference, so a method can use the object's methods to change the very object the caller has.
questions.aside: Java always passes arguments by value; for an object, the value copied is the reference. So `raise()` can change the object, but writing `e = new Employee();` inside it would only redirect its own copy and leave `emp` untouched.

questions.stem: In Figure 4-10, `main()` declares `Employee myEmployee;` and never calls `new`, yet `displayEmployee(myEmployee)` works. Why?

options.text: `getEmployeeData()` constructs one and returns it to `myEmployee`.
options.feedback: `myEmployee = getEmployeeData();` assigns the returned object, so the reference points to a real `Employee`.

options.text: Java automatically constructs an object for every reference you declare.
options.feedback: Declaring a reference never creates an object; `new` must run somewhere.

options.text: `displayEmployee()` constructs it when the object is passed in.
options.feedback: A method that receives an object uses it. Nothing in `displayEmployee()` calls `new`.

options.text: It works only because the fields default to 0 and `null`.
options.feedback: Default values belong to an object that exists. Here the object exists because a method built and returned it.

questions.hint: Which method in the program contains `new Employee()`?
questions.explanation: An object doesn't have to be constructed in the method that declares its reference. It can be constructed elsewhere and returned; constructing it in `main()` too would only be overwritten.

checks.title: Creating and Using Constructors
checks.subtitle: Automatic default values, writing constructors, parameters, and overloading
checks.intro: A class sets its price to 50 in its "constructor," yet every new object reports 0.0. Five questions on how objects get their first values.
takeaways: A constructor has exactly the class's name and no return type, not even `void`. Any constructor with no parameters is a default constructor, whether you write it or Java supplies it.
Java supplies a default constructor only when you write none. It leaves numeric fields 0, `char` fields `'\u0000'`, `boolean` fields `false` and references `null`.
Once you write any constructor, `new X()` with no arguments works only if you also write a parameterless one. Overloaded constructors must differ in their parameter lists.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `0 false null`
options.feedback: No constructor was written, so the automatic one sets the `int` to 0, the `boolean` to `false` and the `String` reference to `null`.

options.text: `0 false`
options.feedback: This assumes an unset `String` is empty. A reference field that refers to no object holds `null`, and printing it shows the word `null`.

options.text: `0 true null`
options.feedback: A `boolean` field starts as `false`, not `true`.

options.text: Compile error: the fields are used before they are assigned
options.feedback: That rule applies to local variables. Fields always receive automatic starting values.

questions.hint: What starting value does Java give a numeric field, a `boolean` field and a reference field?
questions.explanation: When you write no constructor, Java supplies one that sets numeric fields to 0, character fields to `'\u0000'`, boolean fields to `false` and object references to `null`.

questions.stem: What happens when this code is compiled?

code.label: Java

error_contains: constructor Employee in class Employee cannot be applied to given types

options.text: Compile error: the only constructor requires an `int` argument
options.feedback: Once you write a constructor, Java stops supplying the automatic one, so `new Employee()` matches nothing.

options.text: It compiles, and `empNum` is 0 from the automatic constructor
options.feedback: The automatic constructor exists only in classes with no constructor at all. This class has one.

options.text: It compiles, and Java passes 0 for the missing argument
options.feedback: Java never fills in missing arguments. A call must match a constructor's parameter list.

options.text: It compiles, but fails when `temp` is first used
options.feedback: The mismatch is caught by the compiler, so the program never runs.

questions.hint: Which constructors does `Employee` have, and which one does `new Employee()` need?
questions.explanation: After you write a constructor, you no longer receive the automatic default constructor. If the class's only constructor requires an argument, every object must be created with one; add a parameterless constructor if you need both.

questions.concept: No return type, not even void
questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `public void Spa()` has a return type, so it's an ordinary method that nobody calls. Java supplies the automatic constructor, which leaves `price` at 0.0.
This assumes `Spa()` is the constructor. A constructor can't have a return type; adding `void` turned it into a method.

options.text: Compile error: a constructor can't have a return type
options.feedback: Java doesn't see a constructor here at all. A method that happens to share the class's name is legal.

options.text: Compile error: a method can't have the same name as its class
options.feedback: Java allows it, which is exactly why this mistake compiles silently.

questions.hint: Is `public void Spa()` a constructor or a method?
questions.explanation: A constructor must have the same name as its class and cannot have a return type, not even `void`. With a return type, the compiler treats it as an ordinary method, and the class gets the automatic constructor instead.
questions.aside: C# refuses to compile this: a member can't have the same name as its enclosing type (error CS0542). Java permits it, so in Java the stray `void` turns a constructor into a method without any error.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `new Employee()` matches the parameterless constructor, which assigns 999; `new Employee(7677)` matches the one that takes an `int`.
This assumes the no-argument call gets Java's automatic values. Here you wrote a parameterless constructor, and it assigns 999.
This assumes the constructor written last always runs. Java picks the constructor whose parameter list matches the arguments.

options.text: Compile error: two constructors can't share a name
options.feedback: Constructors can be overloaded like methods, as long as their parameter lists differ.

questions.hint: For each `new`, which constructor's parameter list matches the arguments?
questions.explanation: Overloaded constructors let you create objects with different initializing arguments, or none. Java chooses the version whose parameter list matches the call.

questions.stem: You write `Employee()`, which takes no arguments and sets `empNum` to 999. A classmate says it isn't a default constructor, "because default constructors are the ones Java creates." Which reply is accurate?

options.text: Any constructor that takes no arguments is a default constructor.
options.feedback: The term describes the parameter list. Java's automatic constructor is one default constructor; a parameterless one you write is another.

options.text: The classmate is right: only Java's automatic version counts.
options.feedback: This is the misunderstanding the reading warns about. A constructor you write with no parameters is also a default constructor.

options.text: A default constructor is any one that sets fields to default values.
options.feedback: Your `Employee()` assigns 999, not a default value, and it's still a default constructor because it takes no arguments.

options.text: The default constructor is whichever constructor is written first.
options.feedback: Order in the class doesn't matter. The term depends only on whether the constructor has parameters.

questions.hint: What do Java's automatic constructor and your `Employee()` have in common?
questions.explanation: A default constructor is one that requires no arguments. The one Java creates when you write none is a default constructor, and so is a parameterless constructor you write yourself.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.6, Two Truths & a Lie (p. 133), and Don't Do It (p. 153)

checks.title: Learning About the this Reference
checks.subtitle: The implicit this reference, shadowed fields, and calling one constructor from another
checks.intro: A `Student` built with ID 111 and a 3.5 GPA reports `#0` and `0.0`. Five questions on the reference every instance method quietly receives.
takeaways: Only one copy of each method exists. Every call to a nonstatic method passes the calling object's address as the implicit `this` reference, which is how the method reaches the right object's fields.
A parameter or local variable with the same name as a field shadows the field inside that method; write `this.field` to reach the field.
`this(...)` calls another constructor of the same class to avoid repeated code. The reading's rule: only inside a constructor, and only as its first statement.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Student #0 gpa is 0.0`
options.feedback: Inside the constructor, `stuNum` and `gpa` mean the parameters, so each line assigns a parameter to itself. The fields keep their default values.

options.text: `Student #111 gpa is 3.5`
options.feedback: This assumes the left side of `stuNum = stuNum` means the field. The closer, local name hides the field on both sides.

options.text: Compile error: a variable can't be assigned to itself
options.feedback: Self-assignment is legal Java. It compiles and simply accomplishes nothing.

options.text: Compile error: parameters can't share a field's name
options.feedback: Java allows it. The parameter just shadows the field inside the constructor.

questions.hint: Inside the constructor, which `stuNum` is closer in scope: the field or the parameter?
questions.explanation: When a local variable or parameter has the same name as a field, it shadows the field within that method. Unless you write `this.`, every use of the name refers to the local version.

questions.stem: Keeping the parameter names `stuNum` and `gpa`, which body should replace the two lines in this constructor so the fields get the values?

code.label: Java

options.text: `this.stuNum = stuNum; this.gpa = gpa;`
options.feedback: `this.stuNum` names the field of the object being built; the plain `stuNum` is the parameter holding 111.

options.text: `stuNum = this.stuNum; gpa = this.gpa;`
options.feedback: This copies the fields (still 0) into the parameters, which is the reverse of what's needed.

options.text: `this(stuNum, gpa);`
options.feedback: `this(...)` calls a constructor, here the very one it's in, so the compiler rejects it. It doesn't name the fields.

options.text: `Student.stuNum = stuNum; Student.gpa = gpa;`
options.feedback: The class name reaches `static` fields. These fields are per-object, so they need `this`.

questions.hint: Which prefix means "the field of the object being constructed"?
questions.explanation: When parameters share the fields' names, `this.field` identifies the class's field, while the plain name still means the local parameter.

questions.stem: Only one copy of `getEmpNum()` exists. When you call `aWorker.getEmpNum()`, how does it know to return `aWorker`'s number?

options.text: The call passes `aWorker`'s address to the method as `this`.
options.feedback: Every nonstatic method automatically receives a reference to the object used to call it, and `empNum` means `this.empNum`.

options.text: Each object stores its own copy of `getEmpNum()`.
options.feedback: Copying identical code for every object would waste memory. One copy serves all objects.

options.text: It returns the `empNum` of the object created most recently.
options.feedback: The method doesn't look at creation order. It works on whichever object it was called with.

options.text: It returns a shared `empNum` that all objects have in common.
options.feedback: That would be true of a `static` field. `empNum` is an instance variable, one per object.

questions.hint: What does every nonstatic method receive without you writing it?
questions.explanation: Each nonstatic method implicitly receives the memory address of the object that called it, the `this` reference. That's how one copy of the method can work with many objects' fields.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.7, the this reference and Figure 4-18 (p. 135)

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `new Student(3.2)` runs the one-parameter constructor, whose `this(999, avg)` hands both values to the two-parameter version.
This assumes `this(...)` passes along only the argument it received. It calls the master constructor with 999 as well.
This mixes in the parameterless defaults. The 3.2 you passed is forwarded as `avg`.

options.text: Compile error: `this` can't be used before the object exists
options.feedback: Inside a constructor, `this(...)` is allowed: it calls another constructor of the same class.

questions.hint: Which constructor does `this(999, avg)` call, and with what values?
questions.explanation: Writing each constructor to call one master constructor with `this(...)` saves code and reduces errors. Any later rule, such as a GPA limit, is written once in the master version.

questions.stem: Where does the reading allow the call `this(999, 0.0);`?

options.text: As the first statement in another constructor of the same class
options.feedback: `this()` may be called only from a constructor, and the reading requires it to be the constructor's first statement.

options.text: Anywhere in a constructor, as long as no field is used before it
options.feedback: The reading's rule is stricter: if a constructor calls `this()`, that call comes first.

options.text: In any instance method, to reset the object to its defaults
options.feedback: `this.field` works in any instance method, but `this()` can be called only from constructors.

options.text: In `main()`, to create a `Student` without writing `new`
options.feedback: `main()` is `static` and has no `this`. Objects are still created with `new`.

questions.hint: Can an ordinary method call a constructor with `this()`?
questions.explanation: You can use `this` with field names in any instance method, but you can call `this()` only from constructors, as the first statement.
questions.aside: Java 25 relaxed this rule (JEP 513, flexible constructor bodies): statements that don't touch the object under construction, such as checking an argument, may now come before `this(...)` or `super(...)`. On earlier versions, including the one your textbook describes, the call must be first.

checks.title: Using static Fields
checks.subtitle: Class variables shared by every object, static methods without this, and static versus final
checks.intro: A player created first suddenly reports a different team size. Five questions on the data that belongs to the class instead of the object.
takeaways: A `static` field (class variable) exists once per class, and every object reads and changes that one copy. Nonstatic fields exist once per object.
`static` methods have no `this`, so they can't use instance variables directly. Instance methods can use both static and instance fields.

`final` means unchangeable once assigned. A `static final` field must get its value where it's declared; a nonstatic `final` field can be set in the constructor, giving each object its own fixed value.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `#12 of 1`, then `#31 of 2`, then `#12 of 2`
options.feedback: `count` is one shared field. When `b` is constructed it becomes 2, and `a` reads that same field the next time it displays.

options.text: `#12 of 1`, then `#31 of 2`, then `#12 of 1`
options.feedback: This treats `a`'s count as a snapshot taken when `a` was created. All objects read the single current value.

options.text: `#12 of 1`, then `#31 of 1`, then `#12 of 1`
options.feedback: This gives each object its own count. With `static`, there's only one `count` for the class.

options.text: `#12 of 2`, then `#31 of 2`, then `#12 of 2`
options.feedback: When `a.show()` first runs, only one `Player` has been constructed, so `count` is still 1.

questions.hint: How many `count` fields exist, and what is it when each `show()` runs?
questions.explanation: A static field is shared by every instantiation of a class: each object refers to the single memory location. Incrementing it in the constructor makes it a running count of objects created.

questions.stem: What happens when you compile this class?

code.label: Java

error_contains: non-static variable number cannot be referenced from a static context

options.text: Compile error: a `static` method can't use the field `number`
options.feedback: A static method isn't called with an object, so it has no `this` and no particular player's `number` to use.

options.text: It compiles, and the method prints the default value 0
options.feedback: 0 would be some object's value, but a static method has no object to read it from.

options.text: It compiles and prints the most recent `Player`'s number
options.feedback: Java doesn't track a "most recent" object for static methods. The compiler rejects the access.

options.text: Compile error: `number` is private, so the method can't see it
options.feedback: `showNumber()` is inside `Player`, so it may use private fields. The problem is `static`.

questions.hint: When `Player.showNumber()` runs, which object's `number` would it use?
questions.explanation: Static methods have no `this` reference because no object is associated with them; that's why they're called class methods. They can't access instance variables, but instance methods can use both kinds of field.
questions.aside: That's why `main()` is `static`: the JVM calls it before any object exists. To use instance methods from `main()`, you first create an object and call them through it.

questions.stem: Each dog's number of events is set once by its constructor, never changes, and can differ from dog to dog. Which declaration fits?

options.text: `private final int NUM_EVENTS;`
options.feedback: `final` keeps the value from changing after construction; leaving out `static` gives each dog its own value.

options.text: `private static final int NUM_EVENTS = 3;`
options.feedback: `static final` is one fixed value shared by every dog. It can't differ from dog to dog.

options.text: `private static int numEvents;`
options.feedback: `static` makes it one value shared by all dogs, and without `final` it can still change.

options.text: `private int numEvents;`
options.feedback: Each dog gets its own value, but without `final` any method could change it later.

questions.hint: Should the value be one per class or one per object? Should it ever change?
questions.explanation: Static and final answer different questions. Shared but changeable: `static`. Per object but unchangeable: `final`. One shared, unchangeable value: `static final`.

questions.stem: What happens when you compile this class?

code.label: Java

options.text: Compile error: a `static final` field must be set where it's declared
options.feedback: One copy is shared by every object, so a constructor that runs for each new object can't be where it's set.

options.text: It compiles: each `Student` sets `SCHOOL_ID` once, which `final` allows
options.feedback: That's allowed for a *nonstatic* `final` field. A `static final` field isn't set during object construction.

options.text: It compiles, but only the first `Student`'s assignment counts
options.feedback: Java doesn't let the assignment run even once. The compiler rejects it.

options.text: Compile error: `final` fields aren't allowed to be `private`
options.feedback: `private` and `final` combine freely. The problem is where the value is assigned.

questions.hint: How many `SCHOOL_ID` fields exist, and how many times would the constructor run?
questions.explanation: A nonstatic `final` field can be assigned in a constructor. A `static final` field's value must be set at declaration (or in a static initialization block), since resetting the shared value for every object would make no sense.

questions.stem: In `DogTriathlonParticipant`, each constructor adds the dog's total to `totalCumulativeScore`. What happens if you remove `static` from that field?

options.text: Each dog's cumulative score shows only that dog's own total.
options.feedback: Without `static`, each object gets its own copy starting at 0, so each dog adds only its own total to it.

options.text: Nothing changes, since every constructor still adds its total.
options.feedback: The constructors still add, but now each adds to a different field: its own object's copy.

options.text: It no longer compiles, since constructors can't change the field.
options.feedback: Constructors can change instance fields; it compiles and runs.

options.text: Every dog shows the combined total of all dogs created.
options.feedback: That's what `static` provides. Removing it ends the sharing.

questions.hint: After removing `static`, how many copies of the field exist, and what does each start at?
questions.explanation: A running total across all objects needs one shared field. Remove `static` and the class silently gives every object its own copy, so the total stops being cumulative.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.8, You Do It: Using Static and Nonstatic final Fields (pp. 141–143)

checks.title: Using Imported, Prewritten Constants and Methods
checks.subtitle: java.lang, the Math class, import statements and wildcards, and LocalDate
checks.intro: Delivery two weeks after December 25 should land in a new year. Six questions on the classes Java has already written for you.
takeaways: Only `java.lang` (home of `System` and `Math`) is imported automatically. For any other class, use its full path, import the class, or import its whole package with `*`.
`import` copies no code. A wildcard imports the classes in one package but not its subpackages, and `import java.*;` isn't allowed.
Every `Math` member is `static`, so you call `Math.max(a, b)` and never create a `Math` object. `LocalDate` objects come from static methods such as `now()` and `of()`, not from `new`.

questions.stem: What does this program print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `max` of two `int`s is an `int`; `pow` always returns a `double`; `floor` goes down to -3.0; `round(2.5)` gives 3, a `long`.
`pow` returns a `double` even for whole numbers, and `floor` moves toward negative infinity, not toward zero.
`floor(-2.5)` is the largest whole value not greater than -2.5, which is -3.0. `round` returns a whole-number type, not a `double`.
`max` returns the type of its arguments, here `int`. `round(2.5)` rounds up to 3.

questions.hint: For each method, what type does it return, and which way does it round?
questions.explanation: `Math` methods return specific types: `pow` and `floor` return `double`, `round` returns a whole-number type, and `max` matches its arguments. `floor` always moves down, so it's not the same as dropping the fraction.
questions.aside: `Math.round(2.5)` is 3, but `Math.rint(2.5)` is 2.0: on an exact tie, `rint` picks the even neighbor ("banker's rounding"), so `rint(3.5)` is 4.0. Over many values, ties then round up and down equally often.

questions.stem: What happens when you compile this program?

code.label: Java

error_contains: Math() has private access in Math

options.text: Compile error: `Math`'s constructor is private
options.feedback: All of `Math`'s members are static, so you never need an object. Its private constructor makes sure you can't create one.

options.text: It compiles and prints `5.0`
options.feedback: Calling a static method through an object would work, but the object can't be created in the first place.

options.text: Compile error: `Math` must be imported first
options.feedback: `Math` is in `java.lang`, which every program imports automatically.

options.text: It compiles, but fails at run time on `new Math()`
options.feedback: Access to a private constructor is checked by the compiler, before the program can run.

questions.hint: Would you ever need a `Math` object? What stops you from making one?
questions.explanation: Because every constant and method in `Math` is classwide, there's no need for an instance, and you can't make one: its constructor is private. Call members through the class: `Math.sqrt(25)`.

questions.stem: A program uses `Scanner`, `LocalDate` and `Math`. Which is the **smallest** set of `import` statements that lets it compile?

options.text: `import java.util.Scanner;` and `import java.time.LocalDate;`
options.feedback: `Scanner` lives in `java.util` and `LocalDate` in `java.time`. `Math` is in `java.lang`, which is always available.

options.text: `import java.util.Scanner;`, `import java.time.LocalDate;` and `import java.lang.Math;`
options.feedback: This compiles, but the third line is unnecessary: `java.lang` is imported into every program automatically.

options.text: `import java.util.Scanner;` only, since `LocalDate` is in `java.lang`
options.feedback: `LocalDate` is in the `java.time` package, which must be imported. Only `java.lang` comes automatically.

options.text: `import java.*;`, which covers every class in Java
options.feedback: A wildcard works only with a specific package. `import java.*;` doesn't compile.

questions.hint: Which of the three classes is in the one package Java imports for you?
questions.explanation: `java.lang` is the only automatically imported named package. Every other class needs its full path, an import of the class, or an import of its package.

questions.stem: Which statement about `import java.time.*;` is accurate?

options.text: It lets you use any `java.time` class by its short name, but copies no code.
options.feedback: `import` only tells the compiler which names you'll use. With `*`, that's every class in `java.time`.

options.text: It copies every `java.time` class into your program, making it larger.
options.feedback: Despite its name, `import` moves nothing into your program, and a wildcard has no performance cost.

options.text: It also imports `java.time.format`, since that package is inside it.
options.feedback: A wildcard imports the classes in one package, not other packages nested inside it.

options.text: It's a style error that must become `import java.time.LocalDate;`.
options.feedback: Wildcards are common in professional code. Naming each class is an alternative that documents what you use.

questions.hint: Does `import` move code into your file, or just make names available?
questions.explanation: The import statement notifies the program which names it will use; it doesn't copy classes. A wildcard covers one package's classes only, and it can cause conflicts if two packages share a class name.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.9, Importing Classes That Are Not Imported Automatically (p. 146)

questions.stem: What does this program print?

code.label: Java

options.feedback: `plusWeeks(2)` adds 14 days. `LocalDate` rolls past the end of December into January of the next year for you.
This adds 14 to the day number without rolling over. `LocalDate` always produces a valid date.
This moves forward a month instead of two weeks. Two weeks is 14 days.

options.text: Compile error: use `new LocalDate(2024, 12, 25)` instead
options.feedback: `LocalDate`'s constructors aren't public. You create dates with static methods such as `of()` and `now()`.

questions.hint: How many days do two weeks add, and what does `LocalDate` do at the end of a month?
questions.explanation: `LocalDate` objects come from static methods like `LocalDate.of(year, month, day)`, and methods such as `plusWeeks()` handle month and year rollovers that would otherwise need complicated decisions.
questions.aside: `LocalDate` objects are immutable: `plusWeeks()` returns a new date and leaves `order` unchanged. A statement like `order.plusWeeks(2);` on its own line does nothing useful; you must print or store the result.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.9, Using the LocalDate Class and Figure 4-33 (pp. 146–148)

questions.stem: In `LocalDate today = LocalDate.now();` followed by `int d = today.getDayOfMonth();`, which method is `static`?

options.text: `now()`, because it's called with the class name and no object
options.feedback: `now()` is used before any `LocalDate` exists, so it must be classwide. `getDayOfMonth()` needs a particular date.

options.text: `getDayOfMonth()`, because it returns an `int` instead of an object
options.feedback: Return type doesn't decide static. `getDayOfMonth()` is called through `today`, an object.

options.text: Both, because `LocalDate` objects can't be made with `new`
options.feedback: Not having a public constructor only means objects come from methods like `now()`. The objects' own methods are instance methods.

options.text: Neither: `now()` is a constructor, since it creates the object
options.feedback: Constructors are called with `new` and share the class's name. `now()` is a static method that returns a `LocalDate`.

questions.hint: What sits in front of the dot in each call?
questions.explanation: A method called with the class name and no object is static. `now()` and `of()` are static methods that return `LocalDate` objects; methods such as `getDayOfMonth()` work on one particular date.

checks.title: Understanding Composition and Nested Classes
checks.subtitle: Has-a relationships, constructing contained objects, and inner helper classes
checks.intro: A `School` object compiles fine, then crashes the first time it displays its address. Five questions on classes built from other classes.
takeaways: Composition is a has-a relationship: an object of one class is a field of another. The containing class must construct that object, supplying arguments when it has no default constructor.

A nested class lives inside a top-level class, usually as a private helper. Inner and outer classes can use each other's private members, but a nested helper can't be reused by other classes the way a separate class can.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a composition relationship?

options.text: A `School` has a `NameAndAddress` as one of its fields.
options.feedback: When an object of one class is a data field of another class, the classes are related by composition: has-a.

options.text: A goldfish named Moby is a `Fish`.
options.feedback: That's an is-a relationship between an object and its class, from section 4.1.

options.text: A `School` is a `NameAndAddress` with an enrollment added.
options.feedback: A school isn't a kind of address record; it *contains* one. Composition is has-a, not is-a.

options.text: A `NameAndAddress` object is an instance of `NameAndAddress`.
options.feedback: Every object is an instance of its class. That's instantiation, not one class containing another.

questions.hint: Does one class *contain* the other, or is one a kind of the other?
questions.explanation: Composition describes the relationship when an object of one class is a data field within another class, often called a has-a relationship. Any class with a `String` field already uses it.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Java

options.text: `Enrollment 350`, then `Audubon 60618`
options.feedback: `School`'s `display()` prints the enrollment first, then asks its `NameAndAddress` object to display itself.

options.text: `Audubon 60618`, then `Enrollment 350`
options.feedback: This follows the order the fields are declared. Output follows the order of the statements in `display()`.

options.text: `Enrollment 350` only
options.feedback: `nameAdd.display();` is a real call: `School` uses the contained object's public method.

options.text: Compile error: `School` can't call another class's `display()`
options.feedback: `display()` in `NameAndAddress` is public, so `School` may call it through its `nameAdd` object.

questions.hint: In `School`'s `display()`, which statement runs first?
questions.explanation: A class that contains an object can use that object's public methods. The containing class's constructor builds the contained object, and its methods can delegate work to it.

questions.stem: This `School` constructor forgets to build its `NameAndAddress`. What happens?

code.label: Java

options.text: It compiles, then a `NullPointerException` stops it in `display()`
options.feedback: `nameAdd` is an object reference with no object, so it holds `null`. Calling a method through `null` fails at run time.

options.text: It compiles and prints a blank name and a zip code of 0
options.feedback: That would need a `NameAndAddress` object with default fields. No such object was ever constructed.

options.text: Compile error: every field must be assigned a value in the constructor
options.feedback: Java doesn't require this. The field simply keeps its default value, `null`.

options.text: Java constructs the `NameAndAddress` automatically
options.feedback: Java never calls `new` for you, and `NameAndAddress` has no default constructor to call anyway.

questions.hint: What value does an object-reference field hold if no object is ever assigned to it?
questions.explanation: A contained object isn't created by declaring the field. The containing class must construct it, supplying values if it has no default constructor; otherwise the field stays `null`.
questions.ref: Ch. 4.10, Composition (p. 150), and default values in 4.6 (p. 131)

questions.stem: `HouseData`'s field `streetAddress` is `private`, yet `display()` in `RealEstateListing` reads `houseData.streetAddress`. Why does this compile?

code.label: Java

options.text: An outer class can use its inner class's members, even private ones.
options.feedback: Nested classes are packaged together, and they share access both ways: inner can use outer's members, and outer can use inner's.

options.text: `streetAddress` is a `String`, and any class is allowed to read a `String`.
options.feedback: The type of a field doesn't change its access. A private `String` is as hidden as a private `int`.

options.text: It doesn't; private members are visible only inside `HouseData`.
options.feedback: That would be true of a separate class. An inner class's private members are visible to its top-level class.

options.text: Declaring `HouseData` private made all its members public.
options.feedback: A private inner class hides itself from outside classes. It doesn't make its members public.

questions.hint: Where does `HouseData` live relative to `RealEstateListing`?
questions.explanation: An inner class can access its top-level class's fields and methods, even private ones, and an outer class can access its inner class's members. Making the inner class private hides it from every other class.

questions.stem: New `MortgageLoan` and `Appraisal` classes also need street address and square-foot data. Should `HouseData` stay a private inner class of `RealEstateListing`?

options.text: No: a regular class in its own file could be reused through composition.
options.feedback: An inner class is usable only in the class where it resides. A separate `HouseData` could be a field of all three classes.

options.text: Yes: inner classes are the reading's preferred way to share data.
options.feedback: The reading says you usually won't want inner classes; their purpose is a helper used by one class only.

options.text: Yes: other classes can still reach it through `RealEstateListing.HouseData`.
options.feedback: A `private` nested class is hidden from every class except its top-level class.

options.text: No: inner classes can't have constructors, so it must move.
options.feedback: `HouseData` already has a constructor. Inner classes can have them.

questions.hint: How many classes need `HouseData`, and how many can use a private inner class?
questions.explanation: The most common reason to nest a class is that only the top-level class uses it. Once other classes need it too, a regular class used through composition is the better design.
questions.aside: You'll find nested classes inside Java's own library: `java.util.HashMap` stores each key-value pair in a static nested class named `Node`, a helper that no outside code ever needs to use directly.
